planting.note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens for spring bloom; nigella resents transplanting and is best direct sown where it is to flower.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun, since the fine taproot resents disturbance and rarely transplants successfully. Persian Jewels is a classic mixed-color strain of love-in-a-mist, blending sky blue, white, pink, rose, and violet-purple flowers, each one nestled in a delicate, thread-fine haze of feathery foliage that gives the plant its common name. After the flowers fade they are followed by inflated, papery, striped seed pods that are just as ornamental as the blooms and prized for dried arrangements. Nigella grows and blooms fastest in the cool part of the season, going to seed once summer heat sets in, and self-seeds readily where happy, often popping up as volunteers the following year without any replanting.

planting.note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes; celosia thrives in heat and grows fastest during the hottest part of the Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Cramer's Amazon is a giant crested cockscomb selection that produces one of the largest crested flower heads available, a wide, convoluted, brain-like crest that can grow well over a foot across atop a tall, sturdy stem, colored in a deep, rich red-purple. The sheer scale of the bloom makes it a favorite for exhibition growers and for dramatic fresh or dried arrangements, since the dense, velvety texture holds its color and form exceptionally well when air-dried. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture while the crest is forming for the largest blooms, and cut for drying once the crest has fully expanded and firmed, hanging stems upside down in a warm, dark, airy space.

common_name: Black Ball Bachelor Button (Deep Maroon-Black Cornflower)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter Gulf Coast gardens for a bigger, earlier spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

directions: Direct sow seed a half-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Black Ball is a striking cornflower selection bred for fully double, tightly packed blooms in one of the darkest, most saturated maroon-black shades available in any bachelor button, a dramatic contrast to the classic bright blue most people associate with the species. The wiry, upright stems and narrow gray-green leaves are typical of cornflowers, and the intensely dark, almost black blooms make an unusual, sophisticated addition to cutting gardens, especially paired with white or pale pastel companions. Deadhead regularly to extend the bloom period, and expect plants to decline once summer heat arrives, since cornflowers are a true cool-season annual that performs best in spring.

common_name: Painted Lady Sweet Pea (1730s Historic Bicolor Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, training the twining tendrils onto a trellis or netting. Painted Lady is among the oldest named sweet pea cultivars still in cultivation, documented in England since the 1730s, prized for its charming bicolor blooms — soft rose-pink standards paired with white or pale blush wings — and a strong, classic sweet pea fragrance closer to the wild species than many modern, less-scented hybrids. The relatively small, dainty flowers are less showy than modern grandiflora sweet peas but bloom prolifically over a long cool-season window and make outstanding, richly perfumed cut flowers for small bouquets. In mild Gulf Coast winters, sow in fall so vines establish through the cool months for a strong late-winter to early-spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

common_name: Old Spice Sweet Pea (Antique Highly Fragrant Mixed Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Old Spice is a mixed strain of antique, small-flowered sweet peas assembled from pre-1900 grandiflora-type cultivars and selected specifically to preserve the intense, old-fashioned sweet pea fragrance that later, larger-flowered modern hybrids gradually lost in breeding for bigger blooms. The mix produces flowers across the full classic sweet pea color range — pinks, purples, reds, whites, and bicolors — on vigorous climbing vines that bloom over a long cool-season window. Pick frequently for bouquets, since cutting flowers before they set seed is the single most effective way to extend a sweet pea vine's overall bloom period, and enjoy the fragrance indoors, which is often strongest in the cool of morning.
